items.title: Chico Hamilton interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 30, 2000
items.q: How many Count Basie bands did it?

ctx.x: It’s almost like to recreate what that was you would have had to set aside all your experiences from then on to try to get back to that.

Exactly. It’s not putting Fred or Buddy down or putting anybody down, it’s just that I’m a different person. And my newest, the “Timely” album, is living proof of hey, you might not like it as well but hey what the hell, it’s what I’m doing now. Somebody likes it because it’s been moving. And I’m still doing it and I’m still playing all over the world, which is cool. But it’s like how many Benny Goodman bands really did it? How many Count Basie bands did it? How many Duke Ellington bands did it? Regardless of the…

items.title: Chico Hamilton — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I stayed on the band maybe a couple of months and man, we went all the way up to Seattle

ctx.x: And I’ve always been -- I’ve been very fortunate, man. I’ve always worked. I’ve never had really -- I always got a gig. As a matter of fact, man, when I was --more or less put it like this. After I came out of the service, I went back to LA. In the meantime I go back to LA and this is 1945, and the world of music has completely changed, man, completely. Be-bop scene was on the scene. Everybody was out there, from Miles, Diz, Bird, Errol Garner, you name it, Lucky Thompson, everybody, was out in LA and Central…

Well about 15 minutes before the next show, Basie’s all upset, everybody’s really shook up so they sent for Jesse Price. Remember Jesse? So Freddie Green tells Basie, he says evidentially the kid -- if Jo said the kid can do it, let him do it -- because they knew Jesse. And I went on and did the show. I played the shit out of the show, man, and there was not one stitch of drum music but I knew everything, I knew every chart, I knew every solo everybody played on that band. I could sing all their solos, you know,…
I think his father played bass.
